papers.title: Surveying concerns about the future in people with Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BackgroundPeople with Parkinson's disease (PD) experience substantial psychosocial burden, but the extent of their concern about the future is not well characterized.ObjectiveThe objective of the present study is to characterize concerns about the future among people with PD (PwP), with an emphasis on the clinical and demographic correlates of future-oriented concerns.MethodsA survey in the online Fox Insight study platform asked PwP to rate their degree of concern about the future across seven domains: quality of life, disease progression, healthcare needs, social relationships, financial responsibilities, stigma, and specific symptoms. Relationships among uncertainty and demographic and clinical features, such as age of onset, gender, and disease severity, were examined. Latent class analysis was conducted to identify patterns of fear/uncertainty.ResultsAmong 3372 respondents, concerns about the future were common and spanned cognitive, functional, social, and symptom-related domains. Concerns about future cognitive impairment, independence, mobility, and disease progression were most prominent. Women and individuals with young-onset PD reported higher levels of concern than other groups. Latent class analysis revealed two clear patterns, including a high-concern subgroup with elevated worry across nearly all domains. Fewer than half of respondents had discussed these concerns with a healthcare professional.ConclusionFuture-related concerns are common among PwP but is not routinely explored in clinical care. Greater attention to these concerns, especially for young-onset individuals and women, may help clinicians offer more timely and supportive guidance.

papers.title: Sex-related differences in striatal functional connectivity in early Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: A sex-specific pattern within the dopaminergic pathways may underlie the clinical divergences between male and female patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) over the disease course. One hundred forty-seven drug-naive PD patients and 38 controls were enrolled. Anatomical and rs-fMRI images were acquired at baseline. Clinical assessments were performed at baseline and (yearly) at follow-ups for 4 years. Using connectivity-based parcellation, we obtained three ROIs for the sensorimotor, limbic, and cognitive striatal functional subregions, which were used as seeds for functional connectivity (FC) analyses. Baseline and longitudinal clinical data at 4 years were correlated with baseline imaging findings. Female PD showed reduced sensorimotor FC with the superior frontal gyrus compared with male PD patients, while no significant sex-related effects emerged for limbic or cognitive striatal seeds. Compared with controls, PD males and females showed both increased and decreased FC involving the three striatal subregions and frontal, insula, hippocampus, and cingulate areas, while voxel-based morphometry revealed no significant sex-related structural differences. Baseline FC changes in limbic and cognitive striatal circuits were associated with slower motor and cognitive progression over 4 years. Although not supported by formal interaction effects, this pattern may underlie sex-specific vulnerability, possibly reflecting different plasticity responses shaped by biological sex.

papers.title: Nationwide association between proximity to dry cleaners and risk of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Environmental trichloroethylene (TCE) exposure from dry cleaners represents a potentially remediable risk factor for Parkinson's disease (PD). We performed a nationwide, population-based, case-control study to investigate the association between incident PD in U.S. Medicare beneficiaries age ≥67 in 2016-2018 (180,982 with incident PD and 18,848,268 non-case controls) and residential distance to dry cleaners. papers.title: Quantitative biochemical profiling of GCase activity and α-synuclein proteoforms in post-mortem human brains from GBA-related and idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Variants in GBA1, encoding lysosomal glucocerebrosidase (GCase), are risk factors for Parkinson's disease (PD), which is characterized by α-synuclein (αSyn) accumulation and lysosomal dysfunction. Nonetheless, the relationship between αSyn accumulation and GCase deficiency remains unclear. This study aims to quantitatively define the biochemical relationship between GCase and αSyn in GBA-related PD (GBA-PD) and idiopathic PD (IPD). Here, we sequenced GBA1 in 160 post-mortem brains (25 iLBD, 114 PD, 21 controls) and conducted quantitative biochemical analysis of the locus coeruleus (LC), substantia nigra (SN) and gyrus temporalis medius (GTM). We measured Total, Ser129-phosphorylated (pSer129), and C-terminally-truncated αSyn proteoforms, and quantified GCase activity and protein levels. GBA1 variants were detected in 21.9% of PD cases, including a novel frameshift variant. Cortical and midbrain αSyn burden did not differ between GBA-PD and IPD. Importantly, GCase activity and protein levels were substantially reduced in both GBA-PD and IPD across regions, while GCase specific activity was reduced only in the GBA-PD group. pSer129 αSyn burden was inversely correlated with GCase activity, both in the presence (GBA-PD) and absence (IPD) of GBA1 variants. These findings demonstrate a biochemical link between pSer129-enriched αSyn deposition and GCase deficiency across the PD spectrum, supporting lysosomal/GCase-enhancing therapies regardless of GBA1 status.

papers.title: Region-Based Association Between Atrazine and Simazine and Incident Parkinson Disease.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the geographic variation of the relationship between pesticide application and Parkinson's disease (PD) risk. BACKGROUND: Prior studies of PD and pesticides focus on individual pesticides or small geographic areas, limiting their ability to capture nationwide patterns in the presence and strength of the relationship between pesticides and PD. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide study of county-level PD relative risk in Medicare beneficiaries in 2009, and 65 pesticides obtained from the United States Geological Survey. Our outcome was county-level standardized relative risk and our independent variables were estimates of pesticide application from 1992 to 0 2009. We mapped nationwide pesticide-PD associations using Multiscale Geographic Weighted Regression (MGWR) then used regularization techniques with ridge, lasso, and elastic net regression to quantify nationwide relationships between county-level PD risk and pesticides while accounting for multicollinearity. County-level air pollution and rurality were examined as potential confounders. RESULTS: We identified fourteen pesticides demonstrating strong positive geographic associations with PD risk in the Rocky Mountain and Great Plains regions. In nationwide penalized regression models accounting for multicollinearity, simazine (elastic net β = 0.033 per SD) and atrazine (elastic net β = 0.137 per SD) were consistently retained across ridge, lasso, and elastic net. These pesticides remained positively associated with county-level PD risk after adjustment for air pollution. In a sensitivity analysis adjusting for rurality, atrazine remained strongly associated with PD risk, whereas the simazine association was attenuated. DISCUSSION: In the Rocky Mountains/Great Plains region, county-level application of simazine and atrazine is associated with greater risk of PD.

papers.title: Analysis of UBQLN2-Catalyzed α-Synuclein Phase Separation and Fibrillization in Cultured Cells.
papers.abstract: The formation of insoluble α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregates is a hallmark of Parkinson's disease and related synucleinopathies. This protocol describes a robust methodology for inducing and analyzing the intracellular phase behavior of α-syn in human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. Recent studies have highlighted liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and the subsequent "liquid-to-solid" maturation as critical early events in the aggregation cascade of various proteins. A central focus has been the role of ubiquilin-2 (UBQLN2) LLPS as a catalyst for α-syn aggregation. Under oxidative stress induced by sodium arsenite, UBQLN2 undergoes LLPS to form liquid droplets that sequester α-syn, driving its transition into pathogenic fibrils. We outline the comprehensive workflow of this protocol, beginning with the establishment of stable cell lines using fluorescence-activated cell sorting to ensure high EGFP-tagged α-syn expression. We then detail the application of Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching to quantitatively evaluate condensate fluidity and phase transitions. Additionally, an immunofluorescence procedure is provided to characterize the colocalization of α-syn with UBQLN2 and stress granule markers. This integrative approach provides a powerful platform for investigating the molecular mechanisms of protein misfolding in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Salivary-based protein and RNA biomarkers as early diagnostic Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Progressive neuronal degeneration is one of the symptoms of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), which often cause cognitive and physical impairments. In order to start therapy before clinical symptoms appear and to limit the progression of diseases like Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), early screening and diagnosis are crucial. Finding new, accurate and reliable biomarkers is a key objective in recent research in order to facilitate early diagnosis and offer insights into the progression of disease. Compared with invasive, complex, and costly cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) screening methods, salivary analysis has emerged as a promising approach for identifying biomarkers and matrices relevant to assessing NDDs. Compared to other often examined biofluids, saliva collection offers a number of benefits due to its accessibility, non-invasiveness, and suitability for recurrent sampling. These characteristics facilitate early diagnosis and timely treatment of diseases. Current research indicates that β-amyloid (Aβ), tau protein, alpha synuclein (α-syn), DJ-1, and several miRNAs in saliva show potential as biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases. This narrative review addresses the growing need for reliable and standardized saliva-based biomarkers by integrating evidence on biomarker performance with methodological challenges, emerging technologies, and innovative perspectives on multimarker panels, standardization, and validation to facilitate their clinical translation in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

papers.title: Nigral DJ-1 gene knockout in tree shrews can induce phosphorylated α-synuclein aggregation and all key phenotypes of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: DJ-1 is a genetic factor associated with Parkinson's disease (PD), and altered DJ-1 function has been implicated in PD pathogenesis. However, DJ-1 knockout mice fail to reproduce robust PD-like phenotypes or neuropathology, leaving the contribution of DJ-1 deficiency to PD-related disease processes unresolved. To investigate this question in a species more closely related to primates than rodents, we used the tree shrew and performed bilateral, neuron-targeted DJ-1 knockout in the substantia nigra using an AAV-mediated in situ gene editing system. Four out of five DJ-1 knockout tree shrews developed key PD features, including motor abnormalities, substantial loss of nigral dopaminergic neurons, and aggregation of phosphorylated α-synuclein at serine 129 (PSer129αSyn). Notably, one DJ-1 knockout animal did not develop these phenotypes, despite comparable AAV transduction efficiency and DJ-1 knockout levels in the substantia nigra, suggesting that DJ-1 loss may not be solely sufficient in all cases and that additional modifying or compensatory factors may influence disease manifestation. Further pathological analysis showed that PSer129αSyn aggregation was associated with the development of PD-like phenotypes in this model. These findings support a model in which DJ-1 deficiency can promote key PD-like phenotypes in tree shrews, potentially involving PSer129αSyn accumulation, nigral dopaminergic neuron loss, and motor dysfunction. Given that multiple molecular pathways have been proposed to link DJ-1 dysfunction to PD, our results provide in vivo evidence supporting PSer129αSyn aggregation as an important pathological process associated with DJ-1 deficiency. This tree shrew model may therefore provide a useful experimental platform for studying DJ-1-related PD pathogenesis and evaluating potential therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Multimodal AI is Advancing Biomarker Discovery in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's Disease: Evidence, Limitations, and the Translational Gap.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly expanding the biomarker landscape for Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases. Multimodal systems combining neuroimaging, speech, gait, physiological signals, cognitive measures, and molecular markers show substantial research-stage performance. In studies with extractable accuracy and denominator data, reported Parkinson's disease classification accuracies ranged from 94.25% (95% Wilson CI: 93.78-94.68%) to 98.6% (95% Wilson CI: 95.71-99.67%), while Alzheimer's disease diagnostic or conversion-prediction accuracies ranged from 65.8% (95% Wilson CI: 62.54-68.87%) to 99.26% (95% Wilson CI: 97.89-99.75%). Therefore, the field is no longer limited by the absence of candidate AI biomarkers. However, the central bottleneck is translational validation. External validation remains uncommon across medical AI, with rates of 3.7% in high-impact medical informatics studies, 6% in diagnostic medical-imaging AI studies, and 14.7% in ICU AI scoring-system studies. In neurodegenerative disease, many models still rely on single cohorts, internal splits, incomplete metric reporting, and weak linkage between AI-derived digital phenotypes and established molecular or clinical biomarkers. Consequently, performance degradation in real-world populations, reduced specificity, calibration drift, and cohort bias help explain why extensive machine learning activity has not yet translated into routine clinical deployment. In this narrative review, we therefore synthesize quantitative evidence across motor, cognitive, neuropsychiatric, remote-monitoring, and neuroimaging domains. We argue that progress in AI for Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease now depends less on additional model novelty alone than on standardized validation pipelines, external cohort testing, calibration assessment, interpretable multimodal fusion, and clinically meaningful endpoints. Nonetheless, with these safeguards, multimodal AI can move from promising biomarker discovery toward reprod

papers.title: Mechanism of the lysosomal calcium signaling TRPML1-TFEB axis in Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: Apoptosis : an international journal on programmed cell death
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a prevalent chronic neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive apoptosis of midbrain substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons, striatal dopamine depletion, and α-synuclein (α-syn)-positive Lewy-body formation. Patients exhibit motor deficits (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability) plus non-motor manifestations such as cognitive and sleep impairment. PD pathogenesis arises from intertwined mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, defective protein degradation and disrupted calcium homeostasis, whose precise mechanisms remain incompletely defined. As both a degradative organelle and signaling hub, lysosomes govern clearance of proteins and damaged organelles and mediate key neuronal events through calcium-dependent signaling. Transient Receptor Potential Mucolipin 1 (TRPML1), a lysosomal calcium-release channel, and Transcription Factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosome biogenesis and autophagic flux, constitute the conserved TRPML1-TFEB axis that couples lysosomal calcium signaling to transcriptional control of cellular degradation. Physiologically, TRPML1-triggered calcium release activates calcineurin to drive TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, one of several convergent routes that maintain neuronal protein and organelle homeostasis; TFEB is likewise engaged by the second lysosomal calcium channel TPC2, by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) inhibition and by oxidative-stress-dependent phosphatases. Pathological TRPML1 malfunction perturbs lysosomal calcium signaling and suppresses TFEB activity, triggering lysosomal defects, autophagic blockage, α-syn buildup, mitochondrial damage and oxidative stress, which culminate in dopaminergic neuronal death and PD progression. papers.title: Asperuloside ameliorates dopaminergic neuron injury in Parkinson's disease by reprogramming microglial glucose metabolism in part through the AMPK pathway to induce M2 polarization.
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether asperuloside (ASP) regulates microglial metabolic reprogramming and polarization via AMPK signaling to protect dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease (PD). In LPS-stimulated BV-2 microglia, ASP reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), decreased the CD86/CD206 ratio, upregulated M2 markers (Arg1, Chil3, Retnla) and enhanced the activities of SOD, CAT, and GPx. ASP shifted metabolism from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation (reduced ECAR/lactate, restored OCR/ATP, upregulated Ppargc1a/Nrf1), accompanied by increased AMPK phosphorylation and reduced NF-κB activation; these effects were partially blocked by dorsomorphin (AMPK inhibitor). Conditioned media from ASP-treated microglia improved MN9D neuronal viability, reduced apoptosis, and increased PSD95/SYP. papers.title: Therapeutic Potential of Intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation in Central Nervous System Diseases: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Translation.
papers.abstract: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS), a patterned repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation technique, modulates cortical excitability and induces neuroplasticity rapidly. Recently, iTBS has garnered considerable attention for its application in multiple central nervous system disorders. Its effects extend beyond local neuronal changes, propagating across synaptic plasticity, glial responses, neurovascular-immune microenvironment, subcellular homeostasis, and large-scale neural networks, though existing mechanistic evidence remains fragmented. Heterogeneous study designs, varying disease models, stimulation targets, parameters, and observation points, contribute to inconsistent findings. Most research only establishes correlations between iTBS and molecular, cellular, or network changes, failing to confirm causal sequences or cross-level relationships. This review synthesizes evidence from stroke, spinal cord injury, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and depression and anxiety-related disorders, analyzing shared and disease-specific mechanisms across biological levels. This review identifies limitations in causal evidence and dose-response characterization and proposes a multilevel framework for interpreting the reported biological effects of iTBS, with the aim of informing future clinical translation and the optimization of disease-specific stimulation strategies.

papers.title: Quality of life impairment in Parkinson's disease with probable REM sleep behavior disorder is primarily linked to fear of falling and anxiety.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is associated with worse quality of life (QoL) in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, it remains unclear whether this relationship is direct or mediated through specific clinical features. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study including 468 patients with PD. QoL was assessed using the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39). Multivariable linear regression and mediation analyses with bootstrapping were performed to identify determinants of QoL and potential indirect associations between probable RBD (pRBD) and QoL. RESULTS: Patients with pRBD had worse QoL and a more severe clinical profile. Fear of falling and anxiety emerged as the strongest independent determinants of QoL, whereas pRBD was not an independent predictor. Mediation analyses demonstrated that the association between pRBD and QoL was largely indirect, with fear of falling and anxiety accounting for much of the observed relationship. Depression, gait impairment, and voice handicap showed moderate mediation effects, whereas global non-motor burden had a limited contribution. The NMSS mood/cognition domain was not a significant mediator. CONCLUSIONS: The association between pRBD and QoL appears to involve specific clinical factors rather than global symptom burden.

papers.title: Prevalence and Risk Factors of Excessive Daytime Sleepiness in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) is a common but often overlooked condition in older adults, and it is associated with a variety of adverse outcomes. This study aimed to explore the pooled prevalence of EDS and its risk factors among older adults. DESIGN: Systematic review and meta-analysis. SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS: Adults aged 60 years and older in any setting. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in 8 databases, including CNKI, VIP, CBM, WanFang Data, Web of Science, PubMed, Embase, and The Cochrane Library from inception to October 2025. Two researchers independently screened the literature and extracted the information. Pooled prevalence estimates and odds ratios for the prevalence of EDS in older adults and its risk factors were calculated using fixed- or random-effects models. RESULTS: Forty-three eligible studies were included; the overall pooled prevalence of EDS in older adults was 16.9%. Subgroup analyses revealed significant variations in prevalence across geographic regions (P < .001), with the lowest rate observed in East Asia (13.0%) and the highest in Western Asia (21.8%). Furthermore, the use of different Epworth Sleepiness Scale cutoff values resulted in significant differences. Several factors were significantly associated with an increased risk of EDS, including male sex, obesity, malnutrition, urinary incontinence, and various comorbidities (eg, dementia, Parkinson's disease, cerebrovascular disease, depression, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, insomnia, and obstructive sleep apnea). Conversely, the use of hypnotic medications may serve as a protective factor. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: EDS is common among older adults, although prevalence estimates vary across geographic regions and according to the Epworth Sleepiness Scale cutoff used. Several demographic, nutritional, and health-related factors were associated with EDS. These findings support greater clinical attention to EDS and targeted early screening

papers.title: A multi-phasic and symptom-informed model of vocational rehabilitation services for people with Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAs the global prevalence of Parkinson's disease (PD) rises, the demand for vocational rehabilitation (VR) services among individuals with PD is expected to grow.ObjectiveThis article presents a sequential model for serving people with PD across the phases of the VR process.MethodAfter briefly reviewing the etiology, incidence, prevalence, and career development implications of PD, the authors outline direct service and advocacy recommendations for VR professionals.ResultsThe article emphasizes the importance of access to quality health care, adherence to medication and treatment regimens, employer consultation, workplace accommodations and universal design, and collaboration with medical and mental health professionals.ConclusionsRehabilitation professionals should be prepared to address the employment needs of people with PD, particularly those with younger-onset disease who seek VR services to obtain, maintain, and advance in meaningful employment.

papers.title: Safety of Peri-procedural antithrombotic agents in magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) thalamotomy is an increasingly used, minimally invasive alternative to deep brain stimulation (DBS) for essential tremor and tremor-dominant Parkinson disease. Reported intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) as a procedural complication is rare. This study evaluated the safety of briefly interrupting and then resuming anticoagulant/antiplatelet (AC/AP) medications, with resumption on postoperative day one, following MRgFUS thalamotomy. METHODS: In this retrospective study, patients undergoing MRgFUS thalamotomy for essential tremor or tremor-dominant Parkinson disease at a single institution between April 2023 and June 2026 who were taking AC/AP medication were identified. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications were held for five and two days, respectively, before the procedure. Patients were monitored for hemorrhagic complications with immediate post-procedural imaging, a postoperative day-one follow-up call, and outpatient follow-up including 3-month MRI when available. RESULTS: Of 87 patients who underwent MRgFUS thalamotomy during this study period, 50 were taking at least one AC/AP medication; therapy was held perioperatively and resumed on postoperative day one. No hemorrhagic complications occurred in the perioperative period (0/50; 95% CI 0-7.1%), and no old or new hemorrhage was observed in the 33 patients who completed 3-month follow-up scans (0/33; 95% CI 0-10.4%). CONCLUSION: In this cohort, brief perioperative interruption of AC/AP therapy with resumption on postoperative day one was not associated with hemorrhagic complications. These findings support this resumption strategy in similar patients and suggest MRgFUS thalamotomy may warrant further study as an option for patients at elevated risk from prolonged interruption of antithrombotic therapy; larger, prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings and to define optimal AC/AP management strategies.

papers.title: Electrical Stimulation of the Posterior Spinal Cord Horns and its Effect on Gait Kinematics.
papers.abstract: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is often used as therapy for some difficult-to-treat painful conditions. Its analgesic effect is well known, but less studied are its effects on motor function. Single case reports have described improved motor function in patients implanted with neuromodulation for painful conditions. The exact mechanism of action underlying this reported improvement also is not known. This study included 15 participants who had received SCS implantation for persistent spinal pain syndrome and did not have any condition that otherwise limited their locomotion. Hypothesizing that stimulation would affect their gait parameters, we recorded 12 attempts to walk barefoot at each patient's preferred speed, six before stimulation (with pain) and six after stimulation (with reduced pain perception). Kinematic analysis was performed using 10 infrared cameras and force platforms. Retroreflective markers and clusters were attached to the participants for these recordings and the data processed using software. We found significant improvements in gait acceleration, stride lengthening, and range of motion of the pelvis and hip joints. SCS may affect locomotion in the long term in ways that could be associated with reduced fall risk, suggesting benefits for a broader patient population, such as those with Parkinson's disease. Further investigations of motor changes in patients with implanted SCS are needed. Key words Spinal cord stimulation " Gait o Kinematics " Pain o Locomotion " Parkinson´s disease " Neuromodulation.

papers.title: Feedback as automatic dose selection in a basal ganglia-thalamocortical model of adaptive deep brain stimulation.
papers.abstract: We separate the effects of feedback and of stimulation dose in adaptive deep brain stimulation (DBS), using a seven-population firing-rate model of the basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop. A closed-loop advantage may reflect dose rather than feedback. The model has dopamine-dependent gains, delays, a prescribed 20-Hz beta input, and a suppressive input to the subthalamic nucleus set by a saturated proportional-integral (PI) controller on thalamic output. Dose is the command amplitude, and four constant commands are matched to the closed loop on late command, cumulative command, stimulation use, and full-horizon error. An exact window identity for integral action and a convexity condition, under which a constant command is quasi-statically at least as efficient as any time-varying command within the convex range at a fixed state, define when an advantage reflects dose. At five dopamine levels and three horizons, a constant command with equal stimulation use had lower full-horizon error than the closed loop in all 15 comparisons, and the closed loop settled within 0.004 of the constant command required. In a 200-subject cohort varying 20 parameters, including time constants and delays, the individually optimized constant command had lower error than feedback at a fixed state in all 200 subjects. After dopamine fell and recovered, the closed loop had lower error than the best constant after the change in 185, and over whole runs including its start-up, than the best constant for the schedule in 96. In this model, feedback acts as automatic dose selection whose benefit appears when the disease state changes.

papers.title: Comparative Effects of Mindful Yoga and Expressive Arts on Perceived Stress and Whole-Person Health in Individuals With Mild-to-Moderate Parkinson Disease: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: People with Parkinson disease (PD) experience substantial motor, nonmotor, and psychosocial burdens that are often inadequately addressed by pharmacological treatments alone. Mind-body interventions (MBIs), including mindful yoga and expressive arts therapy (EXAT), have shown promise in alleviating stress, increasing quality of life, and improving whole-person health. However, evidence of their comparative effectiveness and underlying mechanisms remains limited, leaving clinicians and patients with little guidance when selecting between these interventions. This study aims to fill this gap. OBJECTIVE: This trial aims to compare the effectiveness of mindful yoga and EXAT in reducing perceived stress, increasing quality of life, and improving whole-person health in people with PD. A secondary aim is to examine potential mechanisms of action, including functional, psychosocial, and gut microbiome-related pathways. METHODS: We are conducting a 2-arm, parallel-group, active-comparator randomized controlled trial. People with PD are randomly assigned to receive either mindful yoga or EXAT, delivered in six 90-minute sessions every 2 weeks. The primary outcomes are perceived stress and PD-related quality of life. Secondary outcomes include PD-related symptoms and broader quality of life. Potential mediators will cover biopsychosocial domains, including biological and physical factors (gut microbiota, constipation severity and bowel habits, and physical activity) and psychosocial factors (self-compassion, self-efficacy, and perceived social support). Motor assessments are conducted using Mon4t and BooGuu Aspire Fall Risk Management mobile apps. Fecal samples are collected to generate reproducible taxonomic and functional profiles of the gut microbiota. Outcomes are assessed at baseline and 3 months, 9 months, and 12 months after baseline assessment. papers.title: Investigating the cost of care among informal caregivers of people with Parkinson's: a qualitative study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: As societies age, the responsibility for elderly care is increasingly shifted to, especially to unpaid family members, partly to reduce public spending on institutional care. There is a limited body of research on the cost of care, with only a few studies focusing on Parkinson's disease. Qualitative research with caregivers may lead to a deeper understanding of the cost of care and contribute to policymaking. This study aims to investigate the cost of care experienced by family caregivers of individuals diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. METHODS: This research uses qualitative methods. The population of this study consists of family members who provide care for people with Parkinson's. Between March and July 2023, semi-structured in-depth interviews were conducted with 15 caregivers who were recruited through purposive sampling. The data were analyzed through deductive analysis. RESULTS: The cost of caregiving is categorized under 4 main themes: (1) care expenses and coverage status, (2) out-of-pocket costs, (3) labor loss, and (4) time spent providing care. Care expenses are frequently expressed by participants in terms of magnitude of expenses, inadequacy of their income, and limitations of overall financial means. Out-of-pocket costs, which include diverse expense items, are classified under three main categories: (1) healthcare and social services, (2) supplies and home adaptations, and (3) housing and transportation costs. Labor loss includes leaving or taking a break from employment, absenteeism, and loss of social benefits. Lastly, time spent providing care is perceived by caregivers as obscure, unpredictable, and variable. CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that the cost of care for caregivers of people with Parkinson's isn't limited to medical spending and is amplified by diverse non-medical out-of-pocket costs, experienced labor loss, and increased caregiving time.
